social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife and two children

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Blurred vision bilaterally — loss of taste. Bilateral subtle facial weakness. Mild dysarthria.
neurological_exam.motor: Symmetric lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 3/5, knee extension 3+/5, ankle dorsiflexion 3/5. Cannot stand without support. Upper extremity 4/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Temperature sensation loss below T4 level — patchy. Pain and light touch relatively preserved distally. Circumoral numbness.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Diminished bilateral patellar and Achilles (1+). Trace bilateral biceps. Plantars downgoing.
neurological_exam.coordination: Limb ataxia — finger-nose dysmetric bilaterally. Heel-shin ataxic.
neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 2.4 L (predicted 4.0 L — 60%). NIF: -30 cmH2O. Sensory loss pattern initially appeared to have a T4 level on temperature testing — raising concern for cord lesion. However, subsequent detailed exam shows patchy rather than sharp demarcation, more consistent with large-fiber neuropathy. URI with macrolide antibiotic treatment several days prior to onset.

patient.chief_complaint: Sudden temperature sensation loss followed by progressive lower limb instability, weakness, diplopia, and circumoral numbness — preceded by URI.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. B. is a 41-year-old civil engineer presenting with a 10-day history of progressive neurological symptoms. He had an upper respiratory tract infection approximately 12 days ago, treated with a macrolide antibiotic, which resolved. On the day symptoms began, he noticed a sudden loss of hot and cold sensation while taking a shower. He then developed progressive instability and weakness in both legs over the following days. He also developed diplopia, blurred vision in both eyes, and lost his sense of taste. He notes circumoral numbness. By day 7 he could no longer stand without support and presented to the emergency department. On initial exam, a temperature sensory deficit appeared to have a T4 level, which prompted emergent MRI spine. He has no bowel or bladder dysfunction and no incontinence. He has no back pain. He has no history of prior neurological symptoms. Serological testing reveals positive IgM antibodies for multiple viruses including CMV, HSV, and EBV — this triple seropositive pattern created diagnostic uncertainty between a primary viral meningoencephalitis and GBS. His NCS/EMG and CSF ultimately clarified the diagnosis.

quantitative_data.pattern: Severe mixed demyelinating polyneuropathy with conduction block — consistent with AIDP meeting GBS criteria; absent F-waves all nerves

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study. 1. Markedly prolonged distal motor latencies bilaterally (peroneal 7.2 ms, tibial 7.8 ms, median 6.4 ms). 2. Severely reduced motor conduction velocities bilaterally (peroneal 28 m/s, tibial 26 m/s, median 38 m/s) with reduced CMAPs. 3. Absent sural SNAPs bilaterally; severely reduced median SNAP (6 µV). 4. Absent F-waves all nerves bilaterally; absent H-reflex bilaterally. 5. Delayed blink reflex: absent R1, delayed R2 — indicating proximal facial nerve conduction slowing. Pattern consistent with severe mixed demyelinating polyneuropathy with conduction block. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, severe AIDP with sensory ataxia (post-URI, probable CMV/EBV/multi-viral trigger)

differential.key_features: No cord lesion on MRI; apparent T4 level resolved to patchy neuropathy; areflexia not myelitis
CMV PCR negative in blood and CSF; CMV antigenemia negative; NCS confirms peripheral demyelination
No periventricular lesions; NCS demyelinating peripheral pattern; acute 10-day onset
No systemic vasculitis features; ANA/ANCA not elevated; NCS generalized demyelination not multifocal

Severe demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with conduction block

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Rising protein on serial LPs — characteristic of GBS evolution

critical_actions: MRI spine is urgent when apparent sensory level suggests cord lesion — exclude transverse myelitis before LP
Recognize apparent T4 sensory level can occur in GBS from patchy temperature fiber neuropathy — MRI normal cord confirms
Multiple positive viral IgM titers are post-infectious cross-reactivity, not triple active viral encephalitis — confirm with viral PCR from CSF and blood antigenemia
Serial LPs may be needed — first LP protein can be normal in first 48h of GBS; repeat at 1-2 weeks shows classic albumino-cytologic dissociation
Avoid macrolides — QTc prolongation risk in GBS with autonomic dysfunction and borderline QTc
contraindicated_actions: Macrolide antibiotics (QTc risk in GBS autonomic dysfunction)
key_reasoning_points: Apparent spinal cord sensory level (T4) in GBS is a recognized pitfall — temperature fiber involvement in peripheral neuropathy can simulate a cord level; MRI spine is mandatory to distinguish
First-day LP protein can be normal in GBS — protein rises over days to weeks; serial LP at 1-2 weeks may be needed to see classic albumino-cytologic dissociation
Multiple low-titer viral IgM (CMV, EBV, HSV) represent post-infectious cross-reactivity or sequential exposures, not active triple viral infection — viral PCR from CSF rules out active encephalitis
Anti-GD1b antibody explains sensory ataxia in GBS — this is the antibody associated with ataxic GBS variants
Delayed facial blink reflex on NCS confirms cranial nerve involvement within the GBS spectrum

red_herrings.data_point: Triple positive viral IgM (CMV 1:80, EBV 1:40, HSV 1:20)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest primary viral meningoencephalitis (CMV, EBV, or HSV) rather than post-infectious GBS
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Low-titer IgM reflects post-infectious immune response; CMV antigenemia negative, CSF viral PCRs negative — active viral CNS infection excluded; NCS confirms peripheral demyelination of GBS

red_herrings.data_point: Sensory loss with apparent T4 level on temperature testing
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest spinal cord lesion (transverse myelitis) requiring emergent cord decompression
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MRI spine shows no cord lesion — temperature fiber involvement in GBS can produce patchy sensory findings that initially appear cord-level; detailed exam shows patchy not sharp demarcation

metadata.difficulty_description: Apparent T4 sensory level simulating cord lesion, triple viral seropositivity mimicking viral encephalitis, sensory ataxia with anti-GD1b — multiple concurrent diagnostic red herrings
